\title{Physics-guided machine-learning prediction of spontaneous energy localization in a sine-Gordon pendulum ring}

\author{Adrian Mittal\\[6pt]
{\small Department of Physics, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA 15213}\\[6pt]
{\small almittal@andrew.cmu.edu}}

\date{}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
In a ring of torsionally coupled pendulums with a global coupling, a nearly uniform swing is destabilized by a type-III instability and, after several swing periods, concentrates its energy on a few pendulums. In earlier work we predicted where this hotspot forms from early-time data, using spatial smoothing and a convolutional and recurrent neural network. Here we start from the physics of the instability. The Floquet growth spectrum of the uniform swing shows that only a handful of the longest ring modes grow, which explains the optimal smoothing width found before. The localization site is fixed by the initial state, so prediction is limited by measurement precision, not by chaos. Guided by the spectrum, we design a small convolutional network built around the symmetry of the ring. At the settings stated in the earlier work, it halves the error of the network used there with a thousandth of its parameters. We also compare different ways of defining the localization site and find that the center of the hump of energy that forms, taken at the moment the first pendulum swings over the top, can be predicted within one pendulum in 99.4\% of runs. Finally, we show that the amplitude and the global coupling affect when and where the energy localizes mainly through the growth spectrum.
\end{abstract}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Spontaneous energy localization, in which a large share of a nonlinear system's energy gathers on a small part of it, is common in nonlinear lattices \cite{sievers1988intrinsic,campbell2004localizing,flach2008discrete}. Because such ``hotspots'' may also matter in structures from micromechanical arrays to bridges and transmission lines \cite{sato2006colloquium,green2006failure,ARIOLI2015901,zhang2017wind}, predicting where they form is of practical as well as fundamental interest. A well-known route to localization is the modulational instability of a plane-wave mode \cite{kivshar1993creation,dauxois1993energy,extreme}, and an instability of type III \cite{cross1993pattern}, which amplifies the longest waves, often leads to catastrophic localization \cite{english2003modulational,thakur2007driven,cuevas2009discrete}. Since the instability is seeded by noise, where the energy localizes depends sensitively on the initial conditions.

In a previous paper \cite{mittal2026jand} we studied this problem numerically in the discrete sine-Gordon model \cite{cuevas2014sine}, realized as a ring of torsionally coupled pendulums with a global coupling that selects an instability of type III. Smoothing the early energy profile with a box-car of about 17 pendulums substantially improved predictions of the localization site, which suggested that the instability is sensitive to energetic clusters rather than to single pendulums. A convolutional neural network combined with a bidirectional long short-term memory network \cite{Hochreiter1997} (CNN-BiLSTM) then located the site within $\pm1$ pendulum in 94.4\% of test cases. We concluded that the network had found features beyond energy clusters, and left it to a future study to tease them out.

Here we look for those features, starting from the linear stability of the uniform swing. Its Floquet growth spectrum tells us which perturbations grow and how fast, and we ask what it implies for each design question, from what to measure to how to train the network. Before each experiment we stated a hypothesis, based on the spectrum wherever it had something to say, in the spirit of physics-informed machine learning \cite{karniadakis2021physics}, and tested it with an ablation that could refute it. We report the choices that did not pay off as well as those that did. We also wanted a predictor that trains in minutes on a laptop and uses measurements that a real chain could provide.

We call the network of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} \emph{v1} and ours \emph{v2}, and compare them on the same test runs at the settings stated in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, a localization threshold of 10\% of the total energy and initial offsets of $\pm0.025$~rad. Retrained at these settings, v1 places 60.4\% of test runs within $\pm1$, against the published 94.4\%; Appendix~\ref{sec:repro} shows that the published accuracy was obtained at an effective threshold of 4--5\% of the total energy and offsets of $\pm0.0125$~rad.

Section~\ref{sec:methods} introduces the model, its growth spectrum and our methods. In Sec.~\ref{sec:results} we first ask what the spectrum explains (Sec.~\ref{sec:physics}), then build the network (Secs.~\ref{sec:arch}--\ref{sec:final}) and examine how the localization site should be defined (Sec.~\ref{sec:target}). Sections~\ref{sec:settings} and \ref{sec:realchain} ask how the settings inherited from Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} enter the problem and what a real chain requires.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Methods}
\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{The pendulum ring}

We consider the same system as in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, a ring of $N$ pendulums with torsional nearest-neighbor coupling and a global coupling to the ring average. In dimensionless time $\tau=\omega_0 t$, with $\omega_0^2=g/l$, the angles obey
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:eom}
\ddot\theta_n = -\sin\theta_n + \gt\,(\theta_{n+1}+\theta_{n-1}-2\theta_n) + \htl\,(\bar\theta-\theta_n),
\end{equation}
where $\bar\theta$ is the mean angle over the ring, indices are taken modulo $N$, and the dot denotes $d/d\tau$. We use $N=100$, $\gt=0.75$ and $\htl=0.5$.\footnote{Section~2.1 of the journal version of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} prints $\htl=0.05$, a typographical error: Sec.~2.3 there and the simulation code use $\htl=0.5$, the value that gives the instability threshold near $A=1.59$ reported there (our Sec.~\ref{sec:floquet}).} Each run starts at rest with $\theta_n(0)=A+\eta_n$, where the amplitude $A\sim\mathcal{U}(1.65,1.85)$ is drawn once per run and the offsets $\eta_n\sim\mathcal{U}(-0.025,0.025)$ independently for every pendulum. The energy of site $n$ is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:energy}
E_n = \tfrac12\dot\theta_n^2 + (1-\cos\theta_n) + \tfrac{\gt}{2}(\theta_{n+1}-\theta_n)^2 + \tfrac{\htl}{2}(\theta_n-\bar\theta)^2 ,
\end{equation}
which assigns to each pendulum the spring to its right-hand neighbor, as in the simulation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand};\footnote{Equation~(5) of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} prints the spring to the left-hand neighbor. The statistics are the same by symmetry, but the labeled site can differ.} the total energy $\Etot=\sum_n E_n$ is conserved. After swinging almost uniformly for several tens of time units, about 57 on average, the ring suddenly concentrates its energy in a hump several pendulums wide, and one pendulum holds more than 10\% of the total, ten times its equipartition share. For pendulums 20~cm long this happens about 8~s after release. We ask how well the early behavior of the ring predicts which pendulum this will be.

\subsection{Linear stability of the uniform swing}
\label{sec:floquet}

Without offsets, every pendulum follows the same swing $\Theta(\tau)$, with $\ddot\Theta=-\sin\Theta$, $\Theta(0)=A$ and $\dot\Theta(0)=0$, whose period is $T(A)=4\mathcal{K}(k)$, $\mathcal{K}$ being the complete elliptic integral of the first kind of modulus $k=\sin(A/2)$. Writing $\theta_n=\Theta+\delta\theta_n$ and expanding the perturbation in ring modes, $\delta\theta_n=\sum_m a_m(\tau)\,e^{2\pi i mn/N}$, we linearize Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}) and obtain for every mode $m\ge1$ a Hill equation \cite{magnus1966hill},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hill}
\ddot a_m + \left[\cos\Theta(\tau) + \htl + 4\gt\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi m}{N}\right)\right] a_m = 0 ,
\end{equation}
whose coefficient repeats every half swing, $T(A)/2$, so that the swing drives each mode parametrically \cite{landau1976mechanics}. The global term adds the same stiffness $\htl$ to every mode except the uniform one, which is the swing itself, and this shift selects an instability of type III \cite{cross1993pattern,mittal2026jand}, in which the longest waves grow first and fastest. Integrating Eq.~(\ref{eq:hill}) over one swing period $T(A)$ gives the $2\times2$ monodromy matrix $M_m(A)$, whose eigenvalue of largest modulus, $\mu_m$, defines the growth rate $\sigma_m(A)=\ln|\mu_m(A)|/T(A)$; mode $m$ grows when $\sigma_m>0$.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig1_spectrum.pdf}
  \caption{Only a few long ring modes grow. (a)~Growth rate $\sigma_m$ of ring mode $m$ (wavelength $100/m$ pendulums) from Eq.~(\ref{eq:hill}), against the swing amplitude $A$; the swing becomes unstable at $A_c=1.577$, and the bar marks the amplitudes in the data. (b)~At $A=1.75$ only modes $m=1$--$5$ grow; the number above each bar is the mode's $e$-folding time.}
  \label{fig:spectrum}
\end{figure}

The uniform swing becomes unstable at $A_c=1.577$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:spectrum}), consistent with the vertical asymptote of the localization time near $A=1.59$ found numerically in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. As the amplitude increases, more long waves become unstable, but in the range used here only a few do. At $A=1.75$ the five longest grow, with wavelengths of 100, 50, 33, 25 and 20 pendulums, and the fastest grows by a factor of $e$ every 8.4 time units, so that during the first 4.5 time units after release, the observation window of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, the perturbation grows by less than a factor of two. Little travels in that window either, as a small-amplitude estimate of the largest group velocity gives about half a pendulum per time unit, or about two pendulums over the window.

We therefore expected the eventual site to depend on the state of the whole ring, whose longest waves are the growing modes, and a predictor to need little more than the projection of the initial perturbation onto these modes; these expectations guide the design below. The ring is also released from rest, so the initial angles $\theta_n(0)$ are its complete state, and everything observed later is a function of them.

\subsection{Simulation, labels and metrics}
\label{sec:pools}

Training some 760 networks requires far more simulated runs than Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} used, so we replaced its run-by-run \texttt{odeint} integration \cite{virtanen2020scipy} with a fourth-order Runge--Kutta scheme \cite{press1992numerical} that integrates thousands of runs at once (step $\Delta\tau=0.05$, with samples every 0.5 time units as before). On 1,000 test runs it gives exactly the same localization site and time as the simulation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, more than ten times faster. Models are trained on up to 100,000 runs, of which the first 60,000 match the training budget of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. A validation pool of 20,000 runs is used for every model choice and a test pool of 20,000 runs only for the numbers we report; the pools are generated with different random seeds, so no run appears in two of them, and inputs are standardized with statistics of the training pool alone. Sections~\ref{sec:settings} and \ref{sec:realchain} also use pools at other settings (Appendix~\ref{app:training}).

Following Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, a run localizes at the first sample at which one site holds more than 10\% of the total energy, $\max_n E_n>0.1\,\Etot$, and its label is that site. We call this the \emph{first-crossing label} and use it, with the offsets above, for every comparison with v1; Sec.~\ref{sec:target} introduces smoother labels and examines the threshold. Distances are measured around the ring, $d(n,n')=\min(|n-n'|,\,N-|n-n'|)$. Reference~\cite{mittal2026jand} scored the accuracy within $\pm1$ because the localized energy spans several pendulums, which Sec.~\ref{sec:target} bears out. This metric also partly rewards a convention, since in 19\% of test runs the pendulum that crosses first changes if the spring energy in Eq.~(\ref{eq:energy}) is split evenly between neighbors, so we also report the mean distance between predicted and true site, the accuracy within $\pm3$, and the share of runs more than 10 sites off, which we call far misses. The test pool resolves an accuracy to a standard error of 0.3 percentage points.

\subsection{Predictors and protocol}
\label{sec:predictors}

The first of three physics baselines, the \emph{box-car} predictor of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, picks the site where a moving average of the site energy peaks, with the width and the time of the snapshot chosen on the validation pool. The \emph{Floquet filter}, which needs no training, evolves the mean-subtracted initial angles through the linearized dynamics, multiplying each ring mode by its response over a whole number of swing periods, computed from $M_m(A)$ at the run's amplitude estimated as the mean of its initial angles, and picks the site where the result peaks. The number of periods is chosen on the validation pool: six on the main pools, and three to 15 on the pools of Sec.~\ref{sec:settings}, for each amplitude bin where these are binned. The \emph{linear ring filter} is the simplest trained model that respects the ring, a multinomial logistic regression whose score at each site is a circular convolution of the initial angles over the whole ring, with amplitude-dependent weights (200 parameters); it is convex, and we fit it to its global optimum with L-BFGS \cite{liu1989limited}. The network of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, v1, takes the site energies at $\tau=0,0.5,\dots,4.5$, each frame paired with the initial angles $\theta_n(0)$, and combines per-frame convolutions with a bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) layer (Sec.~\ref{sec:arch}). It has 26.5 million parameters, and we retrained it in PyTorch \cite{paszke2019pytorch} with the architecture and training procedure of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} (Appendices~\ref{app:training} and \ref{sec:repro}).

Starting from v1's inputs, we first compared architectures and then changed the inputs, the loss and the optimizer one at a time; finally we combined the best choices and reverted each in turn to see which mattered. Inputs, losses and optimizers were compared in shorter screening runs with up to three training seeds (random initializations of the network), and the final model was trained with five (Appendix~\ref{app:training}).

% ===========================================================================
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{What the growth spectrum explains}
\label{sec:physics}

Let us first return to the box-car smoothing of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, whose best width of 17 pendulums was found empirically. The longest wave that a box-car of width $K$ cancels is the ring mode $m=N/K$; a wider box-car also suppresses longer waves, and a narrower one lets shorter ones through. The best width should therefore cancel the first stable mode, $m_c$, while keeping all the growing ones, which gives $K^*=N/m_c$, or $100/6\approx17$ at $A=1.75$, where modes 1--5 grow. This prediction follows the best width measured at seven amplitudes, from just above threshold to $A=1.90$ [Fig.~\ref{fig:physics}(a)]. The energetic clusters identified in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} thus appear to be the growing long waves, seen through a low-pass filter.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig2_physics.pdf}
  \caption{The spectrum explains the smoothing width, and the long modes of the initial state set the site to within a few pendulums. (a)~The best box-car width (dots, with 16--84\% bootstrap ranges; 2,000 runs per amplitude) follows the Floquet band edge $K^*=N/m_c$ (line), where $m_c$ is the first stable mode; the empirical optimum of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} lies on it. (b)~Share of labels that move by more than one or three sites when white noise of the given size is added to the initial angles; the diamonds give the share moved by more than one site when a $10^{-3}$~rad error is placed only in modes $m\le5$ or only in $m\ge6$. (c)~Share of labels moved by more than three sites when the initial perturbation keeps only the modes $m\le M$, or loses the modes $m\le5$.}
  \label{fig:physics}
\end{figure}

Since the localization is seeded by the small offsets of the release, one may ask whether chaos limits how well it can be predicted. Perturbing the initial angles by $10^{-6}$~rad never changes the label [Fig.~\ref{fig:physics}(b)], and neither does halving the integration step, so the label is a deterministic function of the initial state and the best possible accuracy is close to 100\%. Prediction is limited instead by how precisely that state is known. An error of $10^{-3}$~rad on every pendulum moves a quarter of the labels by more than one site, and the same error placed only in the five longest modes moves half of them. Conversely, if only the five longest modes of the initial perturbation are kept, the site stays within $\pm3$ in 91\% of runs, whereas removing them makes the site random [Fig.~\ref{fig:physics}(c)]. The coarse answer is therefore contained in about ten numbers, the amplitudes and phases of the five growing modes, and local detail decides the last site or two.

Of the physics baselines in Table~\ref{tab:headline}, the best box-car reaches a mean distance of 5.07 sites, close to the 5.4 reported in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. The Floquet filter, which grows the measured initial perturbation without any trained parameters, matches the mean distance of v1 (3.12 against 3.14), although it is less often within $\pm1$, and the 200-parameter linear ring filter beats v1 on every metric.

\subsection{A network built around the ring}
\label{sec:arch}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \input{fig_schematic}
  \caption{The two networks. (a)~v1 applies four convolutions to each frame separately, so that each feature sees nine neighboring pendulums of one frame, and combines the frames in a bidirectional LSTM whose input is each frame flattened into 25,600 numbers. (b)~v2 stacks the ten angle frames as channels of a signal on the ring, so that every kernel sees all frames at once; seven circular convolutions with growing dilation let every pendulum see the whole ring, and the same small head scores every pendulum.}
  \label{fig:schematic}
\end{figure}

The network of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, designed before the growth spectrum was known, follows a pattern common in networks for video, extracting features from each frame separately and following them from frame to frame with a recurrent layer [Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}(a)]. Its view of the whole ring comes from the LSTM's input weights, which are tied to particular pendulums and hold 26.2 of its 26.5 million parameters. Since the coarse answer lies in a few long waves that span the ring, while little grows or travels during the 4.5 time units observed, the spectrum led us to expect that the network needs a view of the whole ring more than a model of the sequence of frames. Because the ring has no ends and the dynamics are the same at every pendulum, the network can also wrap around the ring and apply the same filters everywhere, giving one score per site. In v2 [Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}(b)] the ten frames are therefore stacked as input channels, so that every kernel sees all of them at once, and a stack of circular convolutions gives every pendulum a view of the whole ring with a few tens of thousands of parameters. We tested each of these choices separately, with v1's inputs and training budget.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig4_ring.pdf}
  \caption{Seeing the whole ring and scoring every site alike. (a)~Mean test distance of a dilated circular CNN against its receptive field; the horizontal line is the 200-parameter linear ring filter. (b)~Mean test distance against the number of training runs for the two-branch network of Sec.~\ref{sec:arch} with circular padding and one score per site, the same with zero padding (the two curves nearly coincide), and with a v1-style flatten and dense head; the diamond is v1, trained on 60,000 runs. Zero padding costs far less here than in the final model (Table~\ref{tab:choices}), presumably because the global branch is periodic whatever the padding.}
  \label{fig:ring}
\end{figure}

The receptive field, the stretch of the ring that a pendulum's features see, matters most [Fig.~\ref{fig:ring}(a)]. In a circular CNN of four to seven layers with kernels of three sites, spreading the three sites further apart from layer to layer (dilation) widens the receptive field from 9 to 129 sites and lowers the mean distance from 4.79 to 1.54. A network that sees only nine pendulums is worse even than the linear ring filter, which sees the whole ring.

Our first design, the two-branch network, used the fact that the linear growth stage multiplies each ring mode by its own factor. It combined a shallow local branch of circular convolutions with a global branch that multiplies each of the lowest ring modes by a learned complex matrix mixing the channels, a generalization of the Floquet response and the form used in Fourier neural operators \cite{li2021fourier}. The global branch saturates once it includes the unstable band, as expected, but the deep whole-ring CNN does better and gains nothing from it, presumably because deciding which of several growing humps wins is a nonlinear competition across the ring that no linear filter captures.

Scoring every site with the same filters also saves data [Fig.~\ref{fig:ring}(b)], since the network then learns each pattern only once \cite{cohen2016group}. Trained on 1,000 runs, the two-branch network with one score per site already beats its flatten-and-dense counterpart trained on 60,000.

Whether the frames need a recurrent layer turned out to be a closer question than we had expected. A small gated recurrent unit (GRU) \cite{cho2014learning} applied to each pendulum's convolved frames helped the two-branch network, lowering its mean distance from 1.75 to 1.59, but not the whole-ring CNN, which scores 1.54 with stacked frames and 1.57 with the GRU in front. On the validation pool the whole-ring CNN ties with the same network plus the global branch and with the two-branch network plus the GRU, and we chose the simplest of the three, the whole-ring CNN without recurrence.

Feeding the network the field evolved by the Floquet filter, which we expected to leave it only the nonlinear correction to learn, did not help even with only 3,000 training runs; the network learns the linear growth stage from the data alone. Versions of the two-branch network from 2,000 to 115,000 parameters all land within about a third of a site of each other, so the network need not be large, as one would expect if the answer is contained in about ten numbers plus local detail. We did not pursue other families of models, since on a ring with nearest-neighbor coupling a graph network reduces to a one-dimensional convolution, a transformer over sites lacks the locality of the coupling, and reservoir computing \cite{Chaos_Ott_2017,PhysRevLett_Ott_2018} forecasts trajectories, not a single outcome.

\subsection{Inputs and training}
\label{sec:inputs}

Energies were the natural input for v1, since the box-car analysis and the label of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} are stated in terms of energy, but they hold no information beyond the angles, velocities and coupling constants they are computed from. At release, to first order in the offsets, $E_n(0)$ is a shifted, rescaled copy of $\theta_n(0)$, which alone is the complete state (Sec.~\ref{sec:floquet}). Energies are also expensive to measure, since velocities call for a gyroscope on every pendulum or noisy differencing of video frames, whereas one camera can track every angle. We therefore expected the initial angles alone to match v1's inputs, and they did. Frames of angles did better still, both in screening runs of the whole-ring CNN (mean distances of 1.56 for ten angle frames, 1.66 for the initial angles alone and 1.75 for v1's inputs) and on the cleaner labels of Sec.~\ref{sec:target}; the later frames carry no new information, but make the same information easier to learn.

For the loss, v1 used plain cross-entropy over the 100 sites, which counts a prediction one site off as just as wrong as one 50 sites off. Since neighboring sites are nearly equivalent at the level of the label (Sec.~\ref{sec:pools}), we expected soft labels \cite{szegedy2016rethinking}, spread over the neighbors of the true site, to help. They lowered the mean distance in the same screening runs from 1.75 to 1.58 and cut the spread between seeds fourfold, but they also lowered the share of exact hits (from 40\% to 28\% in full-length training), which we had not expected. Regressing a position on the ring did worst, because it averages two competing humps into a site between them. A term for the expected ring distance did not help and made the model hedge at larger weights; we kept it at a small weight, with which the time head was then tested. Since the same growing modes set both when and where the energy localizes, we added a head that predicts the localization time, which helped the site prediction slightly; the binary head of v1, which predicts whether a run localizes at all, adds nothing on undamped chains, where every run localizes. The physics says nothing about the optimizer, and every adaptive optimizer and schedule we tried landed within the spread between seeds; we kept AdamW \cite{loshchilov2019decoupled} with a cosine schedule \cite{loshchilov2017sgdr}.

\subsection{The final model}
\label{sec:final}

The final model [Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}(b)] feeds the ten angle frames of Sec.~\ref{sec:inputs}, taken over the observation window of v1, to the whole-ring CNN of Sec.~\ref{sec:arch}: seven circular convolutions of 32 channels with kernels of three sites, at dilations 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 1 \cite{yu2016multiscale,oord2016wavenet}. A small head, the same at every pendulum, gives a score $z_n$ per site and the probability $p_n=e^{z_n}/\sum_{n'}e^{z_{n'}}$, and a second head, linear in the ring-averaged features, predicts the logarithm of the localization time $\tau_{\mathrm{loc}}$. With $y$ the true site, the loss is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:loss}
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_n q_n\ln p_n + \lambda_d\sum_n p_n\, d(n,y) + \lambda_t\left(\hat\ell-\ell\right)^2,
\qquad q_n\propto\exp\!\left[-\frac{d(n,y)^2}{2w^2}\right],
\end{equation}
that is, cross-entropy against soft labels of width $w=1$ site, plus $\lambda_d=0.1$ times the expected ring distance, plus $\lambda_t=0.1$ times the squared error of the predicted log-time $\hat\ell$, where $\ell=(\ln\tau_{\mathrm{loc}}-\ln57)/0.2$. The model has 22,786 parameters, none of them tied to a particular pendulum, and trains in about six minutes on the same 60,000 runs as v1.

Against v1, v2 halves the mean distance, from 3.14 to 1.49, cuts the far misses from 5.7\% to 1.5\% and raises the share within $\pm1$ from 60\% to 77\% (Table~\ref{tab:headline}), with about a thousandth of the parameters and a quarter of the training time.

We then retrained the final model with one choice reverted at a time (Table~\ref{tab:choices}). The three architectural choices that follow from the ring's physics matter most. Seeing the whole ring is worth 1.1 sites, circular padding 0.9, and one score per site 0.3, the last while cutting the parameters tenfold. Once the architecture is right, v1's inputs and optimizer cost little. The loss matters mainly for the share within $\pm1$, which falls from 77\% to 64\% with plain cross-entropy, for a reason we come to in Sec.~\ref{sec:target}.

Trained on only 1,000 runs, v2 already beats v1 trained on 60,000 (2.42 against 3.14), and since no parameter is tied to a particular pendulum it barely overfits, scoring 1.49 on the test pool against 1.35 on its training runs with no dropout \cite{srivastava2014dropout} and only a small weight decay. The CNN-BiLSTM overfits despite dropout and early stopping (3.00 against 1.62 for one seed).

\subsection{Defining the localization site}
\label{sec:target}

Most of v2's remaining error on the first-crossing label belongs to the label itself. Within one swing the energy of a forming hotspot changes form and shifts between neighboring pendulums, so which pendulum first crosses 10\% depends on the moment in the swing at which the threshold is passed. To average this out we define a \emph{swing-averaged label}. We split each spring's energy evenly between the two pendulums it joins, which gives a symmetric site energy $E^{\mathrm{s}}_n$, and average it over the last 16 samples, about one swing,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:avg}
\bar E_n(\tau_k) = \frac{1}{16}\sum_{j=0}^{15} E^{\mathrm{s}}_n(\tau_{k-j}) ;
\end{equation}
the label is the top site at the first sample at which $\max_n\bar E_n>0.1\,\Etot$. The two labels agree exactly in only a third of the test runs [Fig.~\ref{fig:jitter}(a)]. Trained with plain cross-entropy, v2 misses the first-crossing label by two sites more often than by one, and half of these two-site misses fall exactly on the swing-averaged site [Fig.~\ref{fig:jitter}(b)]. Soft labels hedge between the two candidate sites, which is why they raise the share within $\pm1$ so much.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig5_jitter.pdf}
  \caption{The first-crossing label jitters within a swing. (a)~Swing-averaged site minus first-crossing site on the test pool. (b)~Prediction errors of v2 trained with plain cross-entropy and of the final model (soft labels), both on the first-crossing label, and of the same recipe trained and scored on the swing-averaged label.}
  \label{fig:jitter}
\end{figure}

When the first-crossing label fires, the top pendulum holds 10.3\% of the energy at that instant but only 5.5\% averaged over the preceding swing, while the hump is still growing, and averaged that way the hump is about eight pendulums wide at half height. The 10\% on one pendulum is thus a momentary peak of a wider hump, which stays in place for about a swing after it forms and then drifts. A label at the scale of the hump, the \emph{hump label}, fires at the first sample at which
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hump}
\max_n H_n > 0.15\,\Etot , \qquad H_n = \bar E_{n-1} + \bar E_n + \bar E_{n+1} ,
\end{equation}
and names the center of that three-pendulum window. Its threshold of 15\% was chosen so that it fires together with the first-crossing label, at a median of 54.5 against 55 time units.

\begin{table}[t]
  \centering

  \label{tab:labels}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    Model & Label [seeds] & Mean dist. & Exact & $\pm1$ & $>10$ off \\
    \midrule
    v2 & First crossing [5] & 1.49 & 27.7 & 77.2 & 1.5 \\
    v2 & Swing-averaged [3] & 0.58 & 70.5 & 96.4 & 0.7 \\
    v2 & Hump [3] & 0.27 & 84.7 & 99.4 & 0.4 \\
    v2 & \textbf{Event-timed hump [3]} & \textbf{0.28} & \textbf{86.2} & \textbf{99.4} & \textbf{0.4} \\
    \midrule
    v1 & First crossing [2] & 3.14 & 22.5 & 60.4 & 5.7 \\
    v1 & Swing-averaged [2] & 2.25 & 42.0 & 83.6 & 4.4 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

On the swing-averaged label v2 reaches a mean distance of 0.58 with 96.4\% within $\pm1$, and on the hump label 0.27 with 99.4\% (Table~\ref{tab:labels}). Splitting the springs evenly without averaging over a swing does not help, so the jitter comes from the energy moving within each swing. The design choices of Secs.~\ref{sec:arch} and \ref{sec:inputs} hold on the cleaner labels, except that soft labels stop mattering, and seeing the whole ring matters even more. A four-layer stack that sees only 17 sites triples the mean distance on the swing-averaged label and raises it more than fivefold on the hump label, against 1.6-fold on the first-crossing label.

The hump label still inherits a threshold from the first-crossing label, whose 10\% was set ``somewhat arbitrarily'' in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. An event that needs no threshold is the first pendulum swinging over the top, past the inverted position ($|\theta_n|>\pi$), at a median of $\tau=50$. That pendulum lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center, the site named by the hump label, in 99.1\% of test runs, and the hump label fires after it in every run, a median of five time units later. The first crossing of 10\% comes at about the same time, 5.5 time units after the event, yet v2 places only 77\% of runs within $\pm1$ of it, against 99.4\% for the hump label. To find out why, we recomputed the first-crossing label at thresholds from 3\% to 15\% of the total energy, which moves it from a median of 1.5 time units before the event to 11.5 after it, and trained the final recipe on each (Fig.~\ref{fig:threshold}).

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig7_threshold.pdf}
  \caption{A single-pendulum label is learnable to the extent that it marks the hump. (a)~Accuracy within $\pm1$ of the first-crossing label against its threshold, for v2 (three seeds), v1 (two seeds), the Floquet filter, and the hump center used as a predictor, shifted by the offset that suits each label best on the validation pool (one site at 7--12\%, none otherwise); ``top'' is the label given by the first pendulum over the top. Both networks were retrained for this sweep, so their scores at 10\% differ slightly from those in Table~\ref{tab:headline}; at 15\%, the 1.1\% of runs whose label has not fired by $\tau=150$ are left out. (b)~Accuracy of v2 on its own label against the median lag of the label after the first pendulum goes over the top, for first-crossing labels at 3--15\% (circles), hump labels of Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}) with windows of three, five and seven pendulums and thresholds of 10--20\% (diamonds), and event-timed hump labels (stars).}
  \label{fig:threshold}
\end{figure}

What v2 learns from a single-pendulum label is essentially where the hump forms. At every threshold from 3\% to 12\% its predictions lie within $\pm1$ of the hump center in 90--99\% of runs, and its accuracy on the label is, to within 2.4 points, that of the hump center used as a predictor [Fig.~\ref{fig:threshold}(a)]; across all thresholds the two rise and fall together (Spearman $\rho=0.99$). A single-pendulum label is therefore learnable to the extent that it marks the hump center, which the early state fixes, and it does so reliably only at thresholds passed close to the event. From 3\% to 5\% the label fires within a median of two time units of the first pendulum over the top and lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center in 98.9--99.4\% of runs, and v2 places 99.1--99.4\% of runs within $\pm1$ of it, as it does on the hump label, though with a larger mean distance (0.34--0.40 against 0.27). When the label is read later, at a threshold that the pendulums on the flanks of the hump can also reach, which pendulum crosses first depends on the moment in the swing, because the hump holds its energy in a different form at each moment.

To see how, we split the energy of every pendulum, Eq.~(\ref{eq:energy}), into its four parts at the sample at which each label fires. After the first pendulum has gone over the top, the pendulums of the hump swing over the top and back together. Near the bottom of the swing (the middle quarter of a half period, timed by the uniform swing at the run's amplitude), about seven of them lie beyond the top and move slowly, and the one labeled at 10\% has turned through about a full revolution. Four-fifths of its energy is then held by the global coupling, whose energy $\htl(\theta_n-\bar\theta)^2/2$ grows with the square of the pendulum's twist from the ring average and, unlike gravity, is not periodic in $\theta_n$, so that a single turn stores $\htl(2\pi)^2/2\approx10$ in it, about 8\% of the total energy. The twist is largest for the pendulum that has turned furthest, at the center of the hump, so the energy peaks there, at a median 10.3\% of the total against 7.1--7.6\% two sites to either side, and the 10\% label lies within $\pm1$ of the center in 94\% of the runs in which it fires near the bottom of the swing.

Near a turning point the same pendulums have swung back below the top and move fast. Nine-tenths of the labeled pendulum's energy is then kinetic, and the top of the hump is flat, the center holding 9.2\% and the pendulums one and two sites from it 9.4--10.0\%, so the pendulum that first crosses 10\% is no longer tied to the center. In the 36\% of runs whose 10\% label fires near a turning point, it lies within $\pm1$ of the center in only 32\%, most often two sites away at the edge of the top. The springs hold only a few percent of the labeled pendulum's energy and merely choose the side. With each pendulum owning the spring to its right, the misses fall mostly on the right (45\% two sites to the right, 8\% to the left), since the pendulum at the right edge of the top owns the stretched spring that joins it to the falling flank, whereas at the left edge that spring belongs to the neighbor outside the top. This is why the first-crossing label tends to lie to the right of the hump center and of the swing-averaged label [Fig.~\ref{fig:jitter}(a)]. Splitting each spring evenly spreads the misses over both sides but leaves the contrast between the two phases nearly unchanged (92\% and 34\%).

Since the first pendulum goes over the top within a quarter of a half period after a turning point in 96\% of runs, the phase at which a later label fires is set largely by its delay after the event. The share of runs in which the 10\% label lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center therefore rises and falls with each half swing, from 30\% for crossings 3.5 time units after the event (near the next turning point) to 99\% at 5.5 (near the bottom of the swing) and back to 19\% at 7.5. Labels passed close to the event escape this, because the hump's energy has not yet spread over its top. Of the runs that pass the threshold at the next turning point, two to four time units after the event, the 5\% label lies within $\pm1$ of the center in 98\% (291 runs) and the 10\% label in 28\% (2,405 runs). Over all runs the 10\% label lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center in only 63\%, and v2's accuracy on it, 77.1\%, is the lowest of all the thresholds. At 15\% the label lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center again in 85\% of runs, and in 99\% of the runs in which it fires 6 to 12 time units after the event. By then the hump has narrowed, its center holding a median 15.4\% of the energy when the 15\% label fires, far above the 8.6--8.7\% of the pendulums two sites off.

The hump label depends far less on when it is read [Fig.~\ref{fig:threshold}(b)], since its one-swing average takes in both forms of the energy and it sums three pendulums. With thresholds of 10\%, 15\% and 20\% in Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}), whose averages end a median of 3, 5 and 7 time units after the event, v2 places 99.4\%, 99.4\% and 98.0\% of runs within $\pm1$ of it, against 92.9\%, 77.1\% and 83.7\% for first crossings of 7\%, 10\% and 12\% read at similar delays, so the threshold of 15\% in Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}) did no harm.

The Floquet filter, which is the same for every label, rises and falls with v2 across the thresholds ($\rho=0.93$), and v1 too does far better at 4\% and 5\% (88.5\% and 88.9\% within $\pm1$) than at 10\% (60.1\%). The best threshold for learning, 4\%, with 3\% and 5\% within 0.3 points of it, is the one that marks the first pendulum going over the top, and the accuracy published in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} was obtained at an effective threshold in this range (Appendix~\ref{sec:repro}). Before training we had fixed a rule for choosing a threshold with physical meaning, the smallest share of the total energy whose label fires no earlier than the event in at least 95\% of validation runs and lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center in at least 98\%. No share from 3\% to 15\% passed, since up to 5\% the label fires before the event too often and from 6\% on it marks the hump center too rarely, leaving room only for a share between 5\% and 6\%. Three times the separatrix energy $E_{\mathrm{sep}}=2$, the on-site energy of a pendulum held at the top, is about 5.1\% of the total energy, and its first crossing narrowly passes, as does the first pendulum over the top. We therefore keep the 10\% threshold only for the comparisons with v1.

For the recommended target we let the event itself time the hump label. At the moment the first pendulum goes over the top, we average the symmetric site energy over the swing centered on that moment and name the center of the three neighboring pendulums that hold the most energy, the narrowest window that sums over the top of the hump. This \emph{event-timed hump label} needs no energy threshold and lies within $\pm1$ of the hump label of Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}) in 99.6\% of test runs. Before training on it we had decided to adopt it unless, on the validation pool, it lost more than 0.3 points within $\pm1$ or its mean distance grew by more than 0.03 sites. It did neither, and on the test pool v2 places 99.4\% of runs within $\pm1$ of it, with a mean distance of 0.28 against 0.27 for the hump label (Table~\ref{tab:labels}), so the results obtained on the hump label carry over. Once a label averages over a swing, neither its window nor its timing matters much, as windows of five and seven pendulums give 99.5--99.6\% whether timed by the event or by thresholds of 10--20\% [Fig.~\ref{fig:threshold}(b)].

\subsection{How the settings enter}
\label{sec:settings}

The other settings of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, the range of amplitudes, the size of the offsets, the number of pendulums and the couplings, were also fixed by hand. To see what each means physically, we simulated pools at fixed settings (Appendix~\ref{app:training}) and trained v2 on the event-timed hump label at each.

At eight fixed amplitudes between 1.60 and 1.95, over which $\sigma_1$ rises from 0.042 to 0.183, the first pendulum goes over the top after a median of 120 time units at the lowest amplitude and 33 at the highest, yet this time multiplied by $\sigma_1$ stays between 5.0 and 6.0 [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(a)]. Localization thus takes 5--6 $e$-foldings of the fastest mode at any amplitude (median 5.75 over a pool spanning the whole interval), of the order of the $\ln(1.4/0.002)\approx6.6$ $e$-foldings that a single growing mode needs to rise from the size the offsets give it, about 0.002~rad, to the 1.4~rad that carries a pendulum over the top, consistent with localization by a modulational instability followed by nonlinear focusing \cite{dauxois1993energy,daumont1997modulational}. The amplitude therefore largely sets when the energy localizes, as the amplitude dependence of the localization time in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} already suggested. The time head of v2 predicts the localization time to a median error of 1.5\%, against 5.0\% for the amplitude alone, a gain of only about two time units, so the real prediction problem is where the energy localizes.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig_clock.pdf}
  \caption{The growth spectrum sets the clock and the coarse site (test pools). (a)~Median time at which the first pendulum goes over the top against the $e$-folding time of the fastest mode, at eight fixed amplitudes (circles; numbers give $A$) and for chains at global couplings $\htl=0.3$--0.7 (diamonds); the line is $5.75/\sigma_1$. (b)~Median delay of that time when the offsets of the same runs are scaled by $s$, against the prediction $\ln(1/s)/\sigma_1$, in five amplitude bins. (c)~Accuracy within $\pm1$ of the event-timed hump label for the Floquet filter (filled) and for v2 trained on each condition (open), against the largest offset relative to the distance above threshold, at fixed amplitudes (circles), with scaled offsets in amplitude bins (squares) and on the twin chains at $\htl=0.4$ and 0.6 (diamonds, with their own $A_c$). (d)~Share of runs whose site lies within $\pm1$ of that of the run with the same offsets at $\htl=0.5$ and $A=1.65$, 1.75 or 1.85 (marker shape), against the rms difference of the growth rates of modes 1--12 in percent of $\sigma_1$, for chains at other amplitudes or couplings (colors).}
  \label{fig:clock}
\end{figure}

Without the offsets, the scatter of the release, nothing would localize, since the uniform swing is an exact solution of Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}). Scaling the offsets of the same runs by a factor $s$ between 1/8 and 4 should delay the localization by $\ln(1/s)/\sigma_1$, and the measured delays follow this with a slope of 1.10 [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(b)]. The size of the offsets also moves the site, which stays in place between the stated offsets and an eighth of them in only 37\% of runs. With smaller offsets the growing modes need longer to rise, while the stable modes, whose Floquet multipliers lie on the unit circle \cite{magnus1966hill}, keep their size, so their local detail weighs less when the hump forms and linear theory reaches further. The Floquet filter predicts the event-timed hump label within $\pm1$ in 73\% of runs at the stated offsets and in 87\% at an eighth of them, and across amplitudes its accuracy falls as the largest offset $\eta_{\max}$ grows relative to the distance above threshold, from 89--99\% where $\eta_{\max}/(A-A_c)$ is below 0.04 to 25--35\% where it is about one [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(c)]. A network trained on each condition places at least 98.4\% of runs within $\pm1$.

At $A=1.75$ every wave longer than about 18 pendulums grows, so a longer ring holds more growing modes, about $N/18$, at nearly the same fastest rate. On rings of 50 to 400 pendulums the number of growing modes rises from two to 22, and the share of runs with a rival hump, one at least five sites away with at least half as much energy when the first pendulum goes over the top, from 2.4\% to 71\%. The Floquet filter falls from 77.6\% to 66.0\% within $\pm1$, but a version of v2 trained on each ring, with two more dilated layers (dilations 64 and 128) so that it sees even the longest ring whole, falls only from 99.9\% to 98.8\%, as expected if the hump forms where the growing band focuses the energy \cite{kivshar1992modulational}. A share of the total energy, unlike the event, means something different on every ring. The first crossing of 10\% comes a median of 2 time units after the first pendulum goes over the top at $N=50$, 5.5 at $N=100$ and 20.5 at $N=200$, where it lies within $\pm1$ of the event-timed hump label in only 49\% of the runs in which it fires, and even the hump label of Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}), with its threshold of 15\%, in only 82\%.

The neighbor coupling $\gt$ barely changes the long waves (Table~\ref{tab:robust}), but the global coupling adds the same stiffness to every mode in Eq.~(\ref{eq:hill}) and shifts the whole spectrum, moving the threshold from $A_c=1.38$ at $\htl=0.4$ to 1.78 at $\htl=0.6$. If a chain entered the problem only through its growth spectrum, a change of $\htl$ could be undone by a change of amplitude. For $A=1.65$, 1.75 and 1.85 at $\htl=0.5$ we therefore chose the amplitudes at $\htl=0.4$ and 0.6 whose growth rates differ least from these, by 2--6\% of $\sigma_1$ (amplitudes 1.46--1.66 and 1.85--2.04), and released these twin chains from exactly the same offsets as their references. They localize after 5.4--5.8 $e$-foldings [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(a)], the Floquet filter, computed with each chain's own $\htl$ and $A_c$, falls on the same curve [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(c)], and the site lies within $\pm1$ of the reference run's in 88--98\% of runs [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(d)], against 77--91\% for chains at 0.4 and 0.6 that share only the fastest rate, so the whole spectrum decides where the energy goes. We had predicted that the twins would agree with their references at least as often as chains at $\htl=0.5$ whose amplitude differs by 0.025; this holds at 1.65 and 1.75 and fails by up to 1.5 points at 1.85.

At $A=1.75$, chains whose amplitude differs by 0.01 keep the exact site in 83--84\% of runs, but the twins, about as close in spectrum, in only 62--73\%, so the spectrum does not decide the last pendulum. The difference lies in the stable modes, since a growing mode responds to the initial offsets in a way set by its growth rate alone, whereas a stable mode turns by an angle per swing that depends on the amplitude and the coupling separately.

\subsection{Toward a real chain}
\label{sec:realchain}

A real chain will be observed with noisy sensors, and its parameters will be known only approximately. Since an error of $10^{-3}$~rad in the initial state already moves a quarter of the labels (Sec.~\ref{sec:physics}), we first trained the network on camera-like data, eight angle frames 0.5 time units apart with Gaussian noise on every pendulum and frame, starting the observation at $\tau=0$, 10, 20 or 30. Watching from release, the camera does well up to about $10^{-3}$~rad and degrades beyond, first through far misses, which triple while the share within $\pm1$ hardly changes.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig6_noise.pdf}
  \caption{Waiting divides the sensor noise by the growth of the unstable modes. (a)~Mean distance of the camera setup (first-crossing label; one seed per cell) against the sensor noise $\sigma_s$ divided by the growth of the fastest mode before the observation starts, for observations starting at $\tau=0$, 10, 20 and 30; the four curves nearly coincide up to an effective noise of about $10^{-3}$~rad, and the horizontal line is the noise-free error from release. (b)~Waiting per tenfold noise in four amplitude bins, on the first-crossing and swing-averaged labels (dots, fits; bars, 95\% intervals), against the predictions from the mean growth rate of the growing modes and from the fastest mode.}
  \label{fig:noise}
\end{figure}

Waiting helps, because the growing modes rise above the sensor noise while the noise does not grow. If the fastest mode alone set the pace, as we first predicted, each tenfold increase in noise would cost $\ln10/\sigma_1$, about 20 time units of waiting. The camera's error does depend on the noise and the start time essentially through the noise relative to the grown signal [Fig.~\ref{fig:noise}(a)], but each tenfold increase in noise costs about 25 time units, close to what the mean growth rate of the growing modes gives, and the cost falls as the growth rates rise with the amplitude [Fig.~\ref{fig:noise}(b)]. A likely reason is that white noise enters every ring mode equally, while the site depends on all the growing modes, each of which rises above the noise at its own rate. Having found this on the first-crossing label, we predicted from the mean growth rate 24.8 time units for the swing-averaged label before any later-start run on that label had finished, and measured 25.5. A camera ten times coarser than $10^{-3}$~rad thus catches up with a precise one if it starts watching about 25 time units later, which for 20~cm pendulums still leaves about 3.6~s of warning.

Tracking only every second pendulum costs nothing, with or without noise, and every fourth costs little without noise, but every eighth fails. Its 13 sensors satisfy the Nyquist criterion for the five growing modes, which we had expected to suffice, but at release the stable modes hold about 90\% of the perturbation and alias onto the wavenumbers of the growing ones. One camera tracking every second pendulum to $10^{-3}$~rad, with v2's ten frames from release, scores a mean distance of 1.93 on the first-crossing label, well ahead of v1 with perfect data (3.14), and locates the forming hump within $\pm1$ in 96.8\% of runs. For 20~cm pendulums, $10^{-3}$~rad is 0.2~mm at the bob; we estimate, but have not tested, that one camera at 30--60 frames per second tracking markers on the bobs can reach it.

  \centering
  \caption{Models trained on the nominal chain and tested without retraining on shifted chains (pools of 5,000 runs simulated with their own true parameters) and on the nominal test pool with sensor noise added. Mean distance on the first-crossing label, over the runs that localize by $\tau=150$: nearly all, except at $\htl$ $+10\%$, where 80\% do. The last column describes the growth spectrum at $A=1.75$.}
  \label{tab:robust}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrl@{}}
    \toprule
    Test condition & v1 & v2 & Growth spectrum at $A=1.75$ \\
    \midrule
    Nominal chain & 3.14 & 1.49 & 5 growing modes, $\sigma_1=0.1185$ \\
    Neighbor coupling $\gt$ $\pm10\%$ & 3.26 / 3.39 & 1.97 / 1.97 & essentially unchanged \\
    Global coupling $\htl$ $-10\%$ & 4.36 & 4.25 & $\sigma_1$ $+21\%$; 6 modes grow; $A_c=1.48$ \\
    Global coupling $\htl$ $+10\%$ & 5.91 & 5.53 & $\sigma_1$ $-33\%$; 3 modes grow; $A_c=1.68$ \\
    One pendulum 2~mm longer & 18.9 & 22.9 & the impurity attracts the site \\
    Sensor noise $10^{-3}$~rad & 6.24 & 2.26 & \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Applied without retraining to chains with shifted parameters (Table~\ref{tab:robust}), both networks lose accuracy as the Floquet spectrum changes. A 10\% error in the neighbor coupling, which leaves the spectrum essentially unchanged, costs v2 about half a site, but a 10\% error in the global coupling changes how fast and how many modes grow, and both networks fall to 4--6 sites, so $\htl$ must be known to a few percent. As in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, an impurity strongly attracts the localization. A single pendulum about 2~mm longer, whose restoring term in Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}) is therefore 1\% weaker, pins the site within $\pm3$ of it in 92\% of runs and misleads both networks. Retrained on chains with one random pendulum up to 2\% weaker, v2 finds the impurity from the motion alone, since a longer pendulum swings slightly slower, and reaches a mean distance of 1.06.

Real pendulums also lose energy, and with linear damping the uniform swing decays toward the threshold $A_c$, so a run localizes only if its perturbation has grown enough before then. At a quality factor $Q\ge1{,}000$ almost every run still localizes, at $Q\approx330$ only 71\% do, and at $Q=100$ none do. Retrained on damped chains, v2 even improves, to a mean distance of 0.84 at $Q\approx330$ on the runs that localize, presumably because near threshold fewer and longer modes grow. The binary ``localizes'' head of v1 (Sec.~\ref{sec:inputs}) then becomes useful, telling from the first 4.5 time units whether a run will localize, correctly in 99.5\% of damped runs.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.6\linewidth]{paper_fig_training.pdf}
  \caption{Networks do not extrapolate in amplitude. Accuracy within $\pm1$ of the event-timed hump label at fixed amplitudes (test pools, three seeds) for networks trained at that amplitude, over 1.60--1.95, and over 1.65--1.85, the range of the main pools (shaded); arrows mark values below the axis.}
  \label{fig:training}
\end{figure}

To find out what a network must be trained on, we trained the recipe on the event-timed hump label at fixed amplitudes (Fig.~\ref{fig:training}), at other offset sizes and at other global couplings. A network trained at a single amplitude places 99.5--99.7\% of runs within $\pm1$ from 1.65 to 1.95, and one trained over the whole interval does as well to within 0.6 points; only just above the threshold, at $A=1.60$, does the network trained there gain (98.7\% against 85.8\%). Outside its training range, however, the network trained on 1.65--1.85 places only 90\% of runs within $\pm1$ at 1.90, 50\% at 1.95 and 25\% at 1.60, and the one trained at the stated offsets places 93\% at twice the offsets and 65\% at four times, where networks trained at those sizes reach 99.3\% and 99.1\%.

Nor does a network carry over to another coupling, even one with a matching spectrum. Trained on a twin chain of Sec.~\ref{sec:settings}, v2 places 99.3--99.7\% of runs within $\pm1$, but only 2--55\% of the other twin's runs, with large differences between seeds, although the sites of the two chains mostly coincide. The network trained over 1.60--1.95 at $\htl=0.5$ places 23--47\% of runs within $\pm1$ on the twins whose amplitudes lie in that interval. Since the uniform swing does not depend on $\htl$, this network reads a twin as a chain at $\htl=0.5$ with the same amplitude and predicts where such a chain, released from the same offsets, would localize (within $\pm1$ in 98--99\% of runs); the twin itself localizes there in only 23--47\% of runs, within half a point of how often the network is right, so a network trained at one coupling ignores the coupling and must be trained at the chain's own.

Trained at $N=100$, v2 also carries over only partly to rings of other sizes. It keeps 97.4\% of runs within $\pm1$ at $N=80$, against 99.4\% on its own ring, but on longer rings, which hold more growing modes than it has seen and are longer than its view of 129 pendulums, it falls to 94.3\% at $N=150$ and 89.5\% at $N=400$, its far misses rising from 0.4\% to 9.5\%. The wider version of Sec.~\ref{sec:settings}, trained at $N=100$, carries over far worse (13--30\% within $\pm1$ on rings of 80 to 400 pendulums), presumably because its dilations of 64 and 128, more than half of its training ring, connect pendulums in a way specific to that ring.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}

We have revisited the prediction of where a noise-seeded type-III instability localizes energy in a sine-Gordon pendulum ring, starting from the physics of the instability. Only a handful of the longest ring modes grow, which sets the optimal smoothing width of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, and the outcome is deterministic, so prediction is limited by how precisely the initial state is measured. The features that decide the localization site, the question left open in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, are largely the projections of the early state onto these few growing long waves, with local detail deciding the last site or two. Localization takes 5--6 $e$-foldings of the fastest mode at any amplitude and global coupling, and a change of coupling can be undone by a change of amplitude that restores the spectrum, both for the time of localization and, in 88--98\% of runs, for the site to within a pendulum; only the last pendulum depends also on the modes that do not grow.

Built around the same spectrum, a circular CNN that sees the whole ring and treats every pendulum alike halves the error of the CNN-BiLSTM with a thousandth of the parameters, beats it with 60 times less training data, and needs no recurrent layer. Most of its remaining error on the first-crossing label belongs to the label, since the first pendulum to hold 10\% of the energy is a momentary peak of a hump about eight pendulums wide. Near the bottom of the swing the turned pendulums of the hump move slowly and hold their energy mostly as twist against the global coupling, which peaks at the center, where they have turned furthest. Near a turning point the energy is kinetic instead, the top of the hump is flat, and the label often names a pendulum at its edge. A single-pendulum label marks the hump reliably only at thresholds, like 3--5\%, that are passed close to the moment the first pendulum swings over the top. A label at the scale of the hump, timed by that event, needs no energy threshold, means the same on a ring of any size, and is predicted within $\pm1$ in 99.4\% of runs.

For a real chain, sensor noise can be traded against warning time at a cost set by the mean growth rate of the unstable modes, and in simulation one camera tracking every second pendulum already beats v1 with perfect data. The network must, however, be trained at the chain's global coupling, over its amplitudes and release scatter, and on a ring of its size.

Our comparison with v1 was made at the settings stated in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, close to the threshold at which the first-crossing label is hardest to learn; at the lower threshold and smaller offsets of its published accuracy the gap narrows, to 92.5\% against 99.4\% within $\pm1$. Damping was simulated as linear, sensor noise as white, and impurities as a single lengthened pendulum, whereas a real chain will have small differences at every pendulum and correlated measurement errors. Testing the recommended setup on a bench-top chain is the natural next step.

\appendix

\section{Training details}
\label{app:training}

\textit{v1.} Implemented as described in Sec.~\ref{sec:predictors}, with the defaults of the TensorFlow (Keras) layers used in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} (26,499,205 parameters; Adam \cite{kingma2015adam} at a learning rate of $10^{-3}$, batch size 64, early stopping on the validation loss); training takes about 23 minutes. Some seeds never leave the loss of a uniform guess, $\ln100$; these were repeated with another seed and are not scored. This happened for one of three seeds at the stated settings, one of nine in the threshold study at the stated offsets, and 11 of 14 at offsets of $\pm0.0125$, presumably because the deviations that locate the hotspot are then smaller against the spread of amplitudes.

\textit{v2.} Hidden activations are GELUs \cite{hendrycks2016gelu}, and the per-site head is a circular convolution of kernel 3, a GELU and a $1\times1$ convolution. Training uses AdamW (learning rate $3\times10^{-3}$, weight decay $10^{-4}$) with a cosine decay and 3\% warmup, batch size 256, for 7,050 steps (30 epochs of 60,000 runs), keeping the checkpoint with the lowest validation mean distance, evaluated every 235 steps on 5,000 validation runs. The architecture comparison used the same budget. Screening runs had 15 epochs and three seeds (two for an unknown start, one per cell of the noise and sensor grids), so differences below about 0.1 sites there are within noise. Damping adds a term $-\gamma\dot\theta_n$ to Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}), so that a free pendulum has quality factor $Q=1/\gamma$; every threshold is then a fraction of the energy the chain still holds.

\textit{Further pools.} Sections~\ref{sec:settings} and \ref{sec:realchain} use pools of 75,000 runs at fixed amplitudes, at other global couplings and on rings of other sizes, test pools of 10,000 runs at other amplitudes and couplings and on rings of 80 and 150 pendulums, and the main pools with their offsets rescaled. In these pools labels were searched up to $\tau=300$, except on rings of 400 pendulums, which were integrated only until their event-timed labels (Sec.~\ref{sec:target}) were complete.

\textit{Hardware.} Most networks were trained on one laptop (an Apple M3 Pro, mostly on its built-in GPU), and about a hundred in the threshold and settings studies on a cloud GPU (an NVIDIA L40).

\section{The settings behind the published accuracy}
\label{sec:repro}

We implemented the CNN-BiLSTM of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} in PyTorch with the defaults of the TensorFlow (Keras) layers used there; given the weights of the original Keras model, it has the same 26,499,205 parameters and gives the same outputs. Its data come from a simulator that gives the same localization site and time as the simulation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} on 1,000 of 1,000 test runs, and the only deliberate change is that the input scaler is fitted on the training pool alone. Trained at the settings stated in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, the network places 61.7\% and 59.1\% of test runs within $\pm1$ in two seeds, with mean distances of 3.00 and 3.27, against the published 94.4\% and 1.44; a third seed never trained.

The published accuracy was obtained at a lower effective threshold and with smaller offsets than stated (Table~\ref{tab:repro}). The first-crossing label at 10\% fires about five time units after the first pendulum swings over the top, when the pendulum that crosses first depends on the phase of the swing (Sec.~\ref{sec:target}). Retrained on first-crossing labels at 4\% and 5\% of the total energy, which still mark the center of the hump, and otherwise unchanged, the network places 88.5\% and 88.9\% of runs within $\pm1$. The offsets were also smaller than stated, since the data-generation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} sets a noise level of 0.025 and its simulation code applies a noise level $s$ as offsets $s\,(U-\tfrac12)$ with $U\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)$, so that the training data had offsets $\eta_n\sim\mathcal{U}(-0.0125,0.0125)$. At a threshold of 4\% and these offsets the network reaches 92.5\% within $\pm1$ and a mean distance of 1.69, close to the published 94.4\% and 1.44, although at such small offsets most seeds never leave the loss of a uniform guess (Appendix~\ref{app:training}). The accuracies published in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} were thus obtained with an effective threshold of 4--5\% of the total energy and offsets of $\pm0.0125$; at a threshold of 4\% and these offsets v2 places 99.4\% of runs within $\pm1$ (Table~\ref{tab:repro}).
